q: In 1678, the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens introduced the wave theory of light.
e: True. The new front is the envelope of those wavelets. In 1678 the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens stated the wave theory of light. Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets of the same frequency and speed.

q: In 1678, the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens introduced the particle theory of light.
e: False. In 1678 Huygens introduced the wave theory of light, not a particle theory. Secondary wavelets and wavefronts are wave ideas. Newton was the particle champion of that era.

q: Huygens' principle states that every point on a wavefront may be considered as a source of secondary wavelets.
e: True. Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets of the same frequency and speed. The new front is the envelope of those wavelets. In 1678 the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens stated the wave theory of light.

q: Huygens' principle states that every point on a wavefront may be considered as a source of primary wavelets.
e: False. Huygens' principle treats every point on a wavefront as a source of secondary wavelets. Primary would mean the original source only. The new front is the envelope of those secondary ripples.

q: The new position of wavefront is the envelope of the wavelets.
e: True. Far from a point source a spherical front flattens into a plane front. The new wavefront is the envelope of Huygens' secondary wavelets. The centres of those wavelets sit back on the old front.

q: The new position of wavefront is the center of the wavelets.
e: False. The new wavefront is the envelope of the secondary wavelets, not their centres. Centres would sit back at the old front. Envelope is the forward tangent surface.

q: If the propagating wave with a frequency $f$ is transmitted through the medium at a speed $v$, then the secondary wavelets will have the same frequency and speed.
e: True. propagating and wave have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of propagating would describe a different law.

q: If the propagating wave with a frequency $f$ is transmitted through the medium at a speed $v$, then the secondary wavelets will have half the frequency and speed.
e: False. Secondary wavelets keep the same frequency and the same speed v as the parent wave. Half frequency would change colour; half speed would lag the front. Huygens copies the wave, it does not down-shift it.

q: A wavefront is defined as a surface associated with a propagating wave which is a locus of all points in the wave that have the same phase.
e: True. It stands perpendicular to the rays. Far from a point source a spherical front flattens into a plane front. A wavefront is the locus of points with the same phase.

q: A wavefront is defined as a surface associated with a propagating wave which is a locus of all points in the wave that have different phases.
e: False. A wavefront is the locus of points that have the same phase, not different phases. Same phase is what makes the surface a front. Different phases would be a jumble, not a wavefront.

q: Wavefront is always perpendicular to the direction of propagation or rays.
e: True. Speed of that travel is set by the medium, not by how loud you shout. A wavefront is the surface of equal phase. Rays stand perpendicular to it.

q: Wavefront is always parallel to the direction of propagation or rays.
e: False. A wavefront is perpendicular to the rays, not parallel to them. Rays show the travel direction and stand normal to the front. Parallel would lay the front along the motion.

q: There are two types of wavefront; plane wavefront and spherical wavefront.
e: True. A wavefront is the surface of equal phase. Rays stand perpendicular to it. Far from a point source a spherical front flattens into a plane front.

q: There are three types of wavefront; plane wavefront, spherical wavefront and cylindrical wavefront.
e: False. This chapter counts two types: plane and spherical. A spherical front far from the source becomes plane. A third cylindrical class is not the listing here.

q: The spherical wavefront from a source transforms into plane wavefront when it is far away from the source.
e: True. fs is the frequency the source emits; vs is how fast the source moves through the still medium. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it. A wavefront is the surface of equal phase.

q: The plane wavefront from a source transforms into spherical wavefront when it is far away from the source.
e: False. A spherical wavefront becomes plane when you go far from the source, not the other way round. Far away, the curvature flattens. Starting plane and turning spherical with distance is backwards.

q: The phase angle is the position of a point on a reference circle of a waveform at an instant.
e: True. Phase angle is the angular position of a periodic-wave point on a reference circle at an instant. 0 or 2 pi means in phase; pi means fully out of phase. Linear position along the path is path difference, a different variable.

q: The phase angle is the position of a point on a reference line of a waveform at an instant.
e: False. Phase angle is the position on a reference circle, not on a reference line. The circle turns 2 pi each period. A line would measure path, which is a different variable.

q: The angular position of a point of a periodic wave is known as the phase angle.
e: True. Phase angle is the angular position of a periodic-wave point on a reference circle at an instant. 0 or 2 pi means in phase; pi means fully out of phase. Angular position of a point of a cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The linear position of a point of a periodic wave is known as the phase angle.
e: False. Phase angle is an angular position on the reference circle. Linear position along the travel direction is path. Do not rename length as phase.

q: Path difference indicates the distance between two points measured along the direction of propagation of the wave through the medium.
e: True. Path difference is extra distance along the propagation direction. It is not a sideways gap. m lambda is in phase; (m+1/2) lambda is out of phase.

q: Path difference indicates the distance between two points measured perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave through the medium.
e: False. Path difference is measured along the propagation direction, not perpendicular to it. Sideways separation is not extra optical path. Along-the-ray extra distance is what sets phase difference.
